description: This group was made to join the NASA Space Apps Challenge to become school representatives. This group was found by Oliver Leong and Evangelista Beti, SMK Pujut 1 Arip.
summary:
Mars Radiation Explorer is an interactive tool that helps scientists see how radiation on the Martian surface changes with place and time. Surface dose measurements come from one rover at one crater, and the results are scattered across papers, so it is hard to tell where the data ends and a model must take over.
We built a model from published Curiosity RAD results. Users change surface pressure, solar activity and quality factor, and see the dose rate with an uncertainty band. The tool shows where the model matches measurements, where it is extrapolated and where it is not valid. A table checks it against RAD. A global map turns elevation into pressure and then dose, showing that deep basins such as Hellas should have lower dose. A mission calculator turns the daily dose into a whole-trip total against the 600 mSv career limit, with the biggest ways to cut it.
It matters because radiation is a major health risk for future crews, and clear models and honest limits help scientists decide what to measure next. Every claim links to a source, and values are labelled sourced, modelled or assumed.
details:
Our group built the Martian Map, an interactive sandbox for planning a first Marswalk in Jezero Crater. Its 13 linked modules cover the map, terrain, weather, radiation, water, astrobiology, route planning, communications, power, suit supplies, robot scouts, gravity and body load, and a final Mission Overview. All modules share one mission plan. When a user changes a limit, such as temperature, dust or distance to shelter, every dependent module updates, and the Mission Overview gives a Go or Hold call and shows which check fails.

The project puts scattered Mars data in one place and lets users test “what if” changes. It helps future crews, planners and students understand the trade-offs of a Mars surface walk. Every module has an evidence table linked to published sources, and modelled values and assumptions are labelled, so users can tell what is measured from what is estimated.

We built it in HTML, CSS and JavaScript as one file that runs in any browser. Charts use canvas and SVG, and we wrote our own terrain, orbit and Mars clock models. Python and Playwright handled building and testing, and Claude, an AI assistant, helped write and test the code. It is creative because the modules are connected, users can play with limits, and it ends in a clear decision. We considered safety, scientific honesty, real mission limits and ease of use. The terrain is a prototype model, and the Go or Hold call is advisory only.
